title: S9 — Marine Concrete, Steel, and Durability Science

concepts.title: Salt is the clock on every coastal structure
concepts.mechanism: Salt in the sea air and spray slowly soaks into concrete and reaches the steel reinforcing inside. There it breaks down the thin protective layer around the steel and the steel starts to RUST. Rust takes up more space than steel, so it swells and cracks the concrete off from the inside — 'spalling'. You cannot stop the salt; you can only slow it with thick, dense cover so it takes decades, not years, to reach the steel. On the west, marine-exposed half of this project, that clock is running on everything.
concepts.mechanismPro: Chloride diffuses to the rebar and depassivates it; corrosion products expand ~6× and spall the cover. Buy time with cover (often 2–3 in in splash zones), low-w/c dense concrete, SCMs (fly ash / slag / silica fume), and sometimes coatings or corrosion inhibitors. It is a durability design, not an afterthought.
concepts.hook: Like salt on a car in a snowy climate — you do not stop the rust, you slow it with undercoating and washes. Coastal concrete is that car; cover and a dense mix are the undercoating.

applied.prompt: To hit a number, a sub suggests trimming the specified concrete cover on the marina-facing structures by half an inch. Your call?

options.label: Hold the cover — it is the durability clock; trimming it shortens the structure's life
options.outcome: Right. Cover is not padding — it is the distance the salt has to travel. Cutting half an inch can cut decades off the time to first corrosion. In the splash zone it is the whole ballgame.

options.label: Allow the trim but add a surface coating
options.outcome: A coating helps but wears and gets damaged; it is a supplement to cover, not a substitute. Trading permanent cover for a maintainable coating moves risk onto a future budget that may not exist.

options.label: Allow it — half an inch is nothing
options.outcome: Half an inch is the difference between spalling at year 15 and year 40. On a marine structure it is the single most important durability dimension, and it is invisible until the concrete falls off.

applied.debrief: On the coast, durability IS the design. The same chloride law governs every marine-exposed element — the marina, bulkheads, docks, seaward condos — and cover plus dense concrete is how you buy the years. It ties straight back to curing: a poorly cured, permeable surface lets the salt in faster.

summary: The chloride mechanism governs your entire west half: salt reaches the steel, rust expands 4–6x, the cover spalls, and the cycle runs away. Defense in depth: low permeability, real cover, crack control, then metallurgy and cathodic protection. Plus galvanic couples (dissimilar metals in seawater are batteries) and the inspection regime the HOA inherits. PLAIN: salt + steel + water = a slow explosion. PRO: w/c ≤0.40, 2.5–3 in cover, 316 not 304, anodes on a survey cycle.

sections.heading: The chloride mechanism — know it cold
sections.body: PLAIN: Salt water seeps through concrete's invisible pores until it reaches the steel. The steel's thin protective skin dissolves; rust begins; and rust takes up 4–6 TIMES the space of the steel it came from — a slow-motion explosion inside the concrete that cracks and pops the cover off, which lets more salt in, faster. The splash zone — wetted and dried, salted and oxygenated, over and over — corrodes fastest; permanently drowned concrete actually fares better (little oxygen down there). PRO: chloride ingress → depassivation → expansive corrosion → cover spalling → runaway. Defense in depth: LOW PERMEABILITY first (w/c ≤0.40, supplementary cementitious materials — fly ash/slag/silica fume refine the pores), COVER 2.5–3 in+, CRACK CONTROL (cracks are chloride highways — design and cure to limit them), then optionally coated/stainless bar, inhibitors, membranes.

sections.heading: Galvanic couples and metallurgy
sections.body: PLAIN: Two different metals touching in seawater make a battery — and the battery eats one of them. An aluminum rail on stainless bolts? The rail dies for the bolts' sins. So: match metals, or isolate them with plastic washers and sleeves. And stainless isn't stainless: the cheaper grade (304) pits and fails in chloride service; marine hardware is 316. PRO: galvanic series intuition — the less noble metal sacrifices; isolate or match; spec 316 (not 304 — pits in chloride) at a 25–40% premium that's invisible next to replacement-over-water labor; hot-dip galvanize (not zinc-plate) carbon steel; treatment-rated fasteners for marine timber (modern treatments corrode standard steel). CATHODIC PROTECTION uses the battery on purpose: sacrificial zinc/aluminum anodes bolted to sheet piles and marine steelwork are consumed INSTEAD of the structure, replaced on a survey cycle — a permanent line item in the marina's operating budget.

sections.heading: The regime the HOA inherits
sections.body: PLAIN: Marine structures aren't finished, ever — they're maintained. Someone must look above water yearly, dive below periodically, and measure how fast the sacrificial anodes are being eaten (their consumption rate is a health report on the whole system). Write that regime and its funding into the handover, or it silently doesn't happen until year 15's lawsuit. PRO: annual above-water visual; periodic dive surveys ($10–30K — anode wastage %, scour at structures, bulkhead alignment); chloride/cover surveys on critical concrete at years 5/10; anode design life 5–15 years; the regime and its reserve funding go INTO the handover package (M7/M12) — 'or the marina becomes year-15 litigation' is the KB's exact warning.

quiz.teach: The chloride-to-spall chain is a causal sequence — each step enables the next.
items: Chlorides migrate through the concrete's pore water toward the steel
The rebar's passive oxide film is destroyed
Corrosion begins on the bare steel
Rust occupies 4–6x the steel's volume, straining the concrete
Expansion cracks and spalls the cover
Open cracks admit more chloride and oxygen — the cycle runs away
quiz.explanation: PLAIN: salt gets in, the armor dissolves, rust swells, the cover pops, and everything speeds up. PRO: 'ingress → depassivation → expansive corrosion → spall → runaway' — every marine durability spec (w/c, cover, crack control, metallurgy) attacks a specific link in this chain. (S9)

quiz.teach: Exposure zones corrode at very different rates.
quiz.prompt: Rank the exposure zones of a bulkhead by corrosion aggressiveness.

choices.text: Splash/tidal zone worst (oxygen + chloride + wet/dry cycling), atmospheric zone next (salt aerosol), permanently submerged best (oxygen-starved)
choices.why: Correct — the counterintuitive part is the bottom: drowned steel corrodes SLOWLY because corrosion needs oxygen, and there's little down there.

choices.text: Deepest is worst — more water pressure forces salt in
choices.why: Pressure isn't the driver; OXYGEN is. The submerged zone is the calmest place on the structure, chemically.

choices.text: All equal — salt water is salt water
choices.why: The wet/dry cycling of the splash zone concentrates salt and feeds oxygen with every cycle — it's several times faster than either neighbor.

choices.text: Atmospheric worst — air has the most oxygen
choices.why: Oxygen without constant chloride delivery is only half the recipe. The splash zone has both, refreshed twice a tide.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the worst spot is where the sea slaps and dries, slaps and dries — salt AND air, forever. PRO: 'splash zone governs the design — that's where the bulkhead caps, the 316 hardware, and the survey attention go.' (S9)

quiz.teach: Sacrificial anodes are consumed at a rate the design predicted — deviations are diagnostic.
quiz.prompt: Year-3 dive survey: anodes are 70% consumed against a model prediction of 40%. What does accelerated consumption tell you?

choices.text: Something is drawing more protective current than designed — stray current, coating damage exposing more bare steel, or a new galvanic couple; survey and FIND THE FAULT, don't just fatten the anodes
choices.why: Correct. Anode consumption is the system's fuel gauge — burning fuel twice as fast means the load doubled, and replacing the tank without finding out why treats the symptom.

choices.text: The anodes were undersized — install bigger ones
choices.why: Maybe eventually — but sizing was designed to the modeled steel area. Consumption at 175% of model means the MODEL's assumptions broke somewhere findable.

choices.text: Normal variation — seawater differs year to year
choices.why: Salinity and temperature move consumption by percents, not by 75%. This deviation is a signal, not noise.

choices.text: Good news — the anodes are working hard
choices.why: They're working hard at a job that got bigger without telling you. Find out what grew: damaged coating? a marina tenant's leaking shore power (stray current)?

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the sacrificial metal is being eaten fast because something is asking for more protection — find out what before feeding it more metal. PRO: 'anode wastage is diagnostic: check for stray current, coating breakdown, new couples; survey, then respecify.' (S9)

quiz.teach: Say it like a pro: the hardware spec conversation.
quiz.prompt: The dock contractor proposes 304 stainless hardware at 20% savings over 316. The PRO-register response is:

choices.text: '304 pits in chloride service — it's not a marine grade. Spec stays 316; the premium is invisible next to replacing seized hardware over water in year four'
choices.why: Correct — the metallurgical fact (pitting corrosion of 304 in chlorides), the spec decision, and the lifecycle justification in two sentences.
The words 'stainless steel' cover alloys with wildly different chloride performance. 304's pitting in marine service is exactly the trap the submittal review exists to catch.
Backwards even as a compromise — the splash and spray zones ABOVE water are the aggressive ones. And dock hardware lives in spray by definition.

choices.text: 'Use carbon steel and paint it well'
choices.why: Painted carbon steel in the splash zone is a maintenance subscription with missed payments. Hot-dip galvanizing has roles; dock cleats and hinges aren't one.

quiz.explanation: PLAIN: the cheaper 'stainless' gets tiny deep holes in seawater and fails; the marine grade doesn't. PRO: '316, not 304 — pitting resistance in chlorides; 25–40% premium, priced against replacement labor over water.' The sim's dock-defect event is this substitution slipping through. (S9)

mathProblems.title: The 316 premium
mathProblems.context: Marine hardware package at the 316-over-304 premium — the number that looks large until you price a hardware replacement campaign over water.

mathProblems.title: Coating the sheet piles
mathProblems.context: Duplex coating (galvanize + paint system) prices per square foot of steel — both faces count, and the splash-zone band gets the full system.

decisionPoints.title: Bulkhead alternates: steel + anodes vs concrete panels
decisionPoints.scenario: Final bulkhead system decision, 8,000+ lf: steel sheet pile with duplex coating and sacrificial anodes (cheaper installed, needs the anode replacement cycle and dive surveys forever) versus king-pile concrete panel system (higher first cost, low-permeability marine mix, no anodes — but concrete's own chloride clock runs on cover and crack control). The QS has first costs; the coastal engineer insists on a 40-year lifecycle model.

options.label: Decide on the 40-year model: first cost + maintenance regime (anodes, surveys, coating renewal vs chloride/cover surveys and joint care) + repair ACCESS costs — and write whichever regime wins into the HOA's funded handover
options.outcome: The model, not the bid tab, picks the system — and either answer is defensible ONLY with its maintenance regime funded and transferred. The unfunded version of either system is the same year-15 litigation with different rust.

options.label: Steel on first cost; the HOA can figure out maintenance later
options.outcome: The anode cycle and dive surveys aren't optional extras on a steel system — they ARE the system. Unfunded, the anodes waste out silently around year 8, the steel starts paying the corrosion bill itself, and 'later' turns out to mean a special assessment with your name in the recitals.

options.label: Concrete panels everywhere — no anodes, no dive surveys, done
options.outcome: 'Maintenance-free' concrete is a marketing phrase, not a material property: its chloride clock runs on cover execution and crack behavior, and it still needs the year-5/10 surveys. You've paid the premium and kept most of the obligation — acceptable, if you knew that going in.

decisionPoints.debrief: Marine structures are systems-plus-regimes: the bulkhead you buy includes the inspections and consumables it needs forever. Lifecycle modeling picks the system; handover funding keeps it alive; and 'maintenance-free' is not a thing the splash zone sells. (S9, M5, M7)
